newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Africa getting economic house in order - IMF.
newsitem.headline: Africa getting economic house in order - IMF.

text.p: Sub-Saharan Africa has made substantial progress towards macro-economic stability, with growth improving and inflation falling, Alassane Ouattara, deputy managing director of the IMF, said on Wednesday.
Average real growth had increased from under one percent in 1992 to over 5.5 percent in 1996 and this trend was expected to continue.
At the same time, average inflation is expected to fall from a peak of 60 percent in 1994 to 17 percent in 1997, he told a World Economic Forum conference in Zimbabwe.
The continent's external current account deficit had also fallen from 15.5 percent of GDP in 1992 to about nine percent projected for this year.

South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said the 12 nations of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) had led the way in reforming their economies with all but Zimbabwe and Swaziland having budget deficits of under six percent of GDP.
"Macro-economic stability has largely been achieved with inflation being reduced in all SADC countries duing 1996, he said. "The change has been phenomenal."
However sub-Saharan Africa still faced serious economic challenges including a very low savings ratio and an overdependence on fast dimishing aid flows, he said.
